Garden rules

A few
ground rules.

This is how I imagine the shared garden would work. People should know who makes decisions and what happens to their writing.

01Choose what you share.

Use a name, a nickname, or no name. Browse without contributing. In the future commons, your relationships and memories are yours to keep, move, or erase.

02Make it accessible.

The imagined network can be entered through a public greenhouse, a screen reader, or an old phone. Text, sound, and touch offer different doorways. Community stewards help translate; no one has to surrender their language to be understood.

03No likes or rankings.

Asking for help is a contribution. Quiet presence counts, too. Seeds have no follower counts, popularity scores, or pressure to keep a streak. Community decisions must include people who have the least time to volunteer.

04Decide who looks after it.

Residents choose paid stewards, publish the rules, and can appeal decisions. Consent is required before sharing another person’s story. Harm needs accountable responses; a beautiful interface alone cannot make a community safe.

05Use resources carefully.

Neighborhood relays use repairable hardware and share energy budgets openly. The future network rests when resources are scarce. Communities decide what stays available offline. Connection should leave room for life beyond the screen.

A speculative path from here to there

How this might come about.

2026

Imagine a different default.

Start with a question: what would the web feel like if belonging mattered more than attention?

2045

Bring the network home.

In this imagined timeline, libraries and gardens become shared access points, stewarded by their neighborhoods.

2086

Let a thousand gardens connect.

Local commons form a planetary network. Knowledge travels freely; communities retain a say in their own futures.

About this project.

This is a speculative design, not a live community service. The people and founding seeds are fictional. Planting, adding chapters, and pocketing work locally in your browser; they do not contact anyone. A seed becomes a bud after one added chapter and a flower after two. Further chapters remain part of its story; nothing withers if you take a break. Hosting may involve ordinary server logs, but this project adds no tracking scripts.

Keyboard navigation, text alternatives, motion controls, and opt-in sound are part of this prototype. A real commons would also need participatory research, language support, paid moderation, and testing with disabled users. Those parts would need to be developed with the people using it.

The design takes inspiration from Low-tech Magazine’s lightweight solar website and Library of Things’ neighborhood sharing model. Seed libraries and greenhouse architecture inform the visual world; all botanical illustrations are original SVG artwork.
